latin: हरिमन्थस्य विदलं हिङ्गुजीरकमिश्रितम् । लवणेन च संयुक्तमार्द्रकेण समन्वितम् ॥ १३९१ ॥ वेष्टयित्वा गोलकेन वेष्टिका खर्परे पचेत् । विदलं चणकस्यैवं पूर्वसम्भारसंस्कृतम् ॥ १३९२ ॥ ताप्यां तैलविलिप्तायां धोसकान्विपचेद्बुधः । माषस्य राजमाषस्य वट्टाणस्य च धोसकान् ॥ १३९३ ॥ अनेनैव प्रकारेण विपचेत्पाकतत्त्ववित् ।
english: Split *harimantha* — chickpea — mixed with asafoetida and cumin, joined with salt and accompanied by fresh ginger: having wrapped it up with a dough-ball, one should cook the *veṣṭikā* on an earthenware pan (*kharpara*). Split chickpea, prepared in this same way with the seasonings named before — on a griddle-plate (*tāpī*) smeared with oil the wise man should cook *dhosakas*. *Dhosakas* of black gram, of *rāja-māṣa* [the cowpea], and of *vaṭṭāṇa* [the pea] the knower of the essence of cooking should cook by this very same method. [The dish is *dhosaka*: the edition prints `धोसकान्` in both halves of 1393 with no variant recorded — the Sanskritized form of the word behind Kannada *dose* and Tamil *tōcai*. At 1393a the manuscripts have `तैले` and the editor corrects to `तैल-`. Note that only the *veṣṭikā* is wrapped in dough, and only the *dhosaka* gets an oiled griddle.]

latin: वट्टाणकस्य विदलं विदलं चणकस्य च ॥ १३९४ ॥ चूर्णितं वारिणा सार्धं सर्पिषा परिभावितम् । सैन्धवेन च संयुक्तं कण्डुना परिघट्टितम् ॥ १३९५ ॥ निष्पावचूर्णसंयुक्तं पेषण्यां च प्रसारितम् । कटाहे तैलसंपूर्णे कटकर्णान्प्रपाचयेत् ॥ १३९६ ॥ यावद्बुद्बुदसंकाशा भवन्ति कनकत्विषः ।
english: Split *vaṭṭāṇaka* [pea] and split chickpea: reduced to powder, then slaked with water, thoroughly permeated with ghee, joined with rock salt, worked about with a *kaṇḍu*, joined with *niṣpāva* [lablab] flour, and spread out on the grinding stone — in a cauldron brimming with oil one should fry the *kaṭakarṇas* right through, until they come out like bubbles, with the sheen of gold. [`कण्डुना` is an implement in the instrumental, printed with no variant: either *kandu*, an iron pan, or an instrument-noun from √*kaṇḍ*, to pound. `चूर्णितं` means the pulses are milled dry and the water added afterwards. Nothing here sours or rests the mixture; the bubbles are a frying cue.]

latin: माषस्य विदलान्क्लिन्नान्निस्तुषान्हस्तलोडनैः ॥ १३९७ ॥ ततः सम्पेष्य पेषण्यां सम्भारेण विमिश्रितान् । स्थाल्यां विमर्द्य बहुशः स्थापयेत्तदहस्ततः ॥ १३९८ ॥ आम्लीभूतं माषपिष्टं वैटिकासु विनिक्षिपेत् । वस्त्रगर्भाभिरन्याभिः पिधाय परिपाचयेत् ॥ १३९९ ॥ अवतार्यात्र मरिचं चूर्णितं विकिरेदनु । घृताक्तान्हिङ्गुसर्पिर्भ्यां जीरकेण च धूपयेत् ॥ १४०० ॥ सुशीता धवलाः श्लक्ष्णा एता इडेरिका वराः ।
english: Split black gram, soaked and freed of its husks by rubbing with the hands; then, ground on the grinding stone, mixed with the seasoning-mix (*sambhāra*), worked over many times in a pot, and after that set aside for that day. Once the black-gram paste has turned sour, one should put it into *vaiṭikā* moulds, cover them over with others that have cloth inside, and cook it right through. Having taken them off the fire, one should then scatter powdered pepper over them; and, smeared with ghee, one should smoke them with asafoetida-and-ghee and with cumin. Well cooled, white, and smooth — these are the excellent *iḍerikās*. [1399c reads `वस्त्रगर्भाभिरन्याभिः`, "with others having cloth inside": the covering moulds are cloth-lined, which is moist heat. `वैटिकासु` is printed with no variant; the sense "in small cups" rests on the locative plus the covering vessels. The finishing order is off the fire, then pepper, then a ghee smear, then the smoking — three separate operations. `धूप-` is literal smoke throughout the chapter.]

latin: तस्यैव माषपिष्टस्य गोलकान्विस्तृतान्घनान् ॥ १४०१ ॥ पञ्चभिः सप्तभिर्वापि छिद्रैश्च परिशोभितान् । तप्ततैले पचेद्यावल्लौहित्यं तेषु जायते ॥ १४०२ ॥ घारिकासंज्ञया ख्याता भक्ष्येषु सुमनोहराः ।
english: Of that very same black-gram paste, balls — spread out broad and thick, and adorned with five holes, or else with seven: one should fry them in hot oil until a redness arises in them. Known by the name *ghārikā*, they are the most delightful among *bhakṣyas*. [*Bhakṣya* is the second of the five classes of food set out at 1344–45. The batter is the soured *iḍerikā* batter of 1399, and the colour contrast is deliberate: steamed, the same paste comes out `धवलाः`, white; fried, `लौहित्यं`, red.]

latin: निच्छिद्रा घारिकाः पक्वा मथिते शर्करायुते ॥ १४०३ ॥ एलामरिचसंयुक्ते निक्षिप्ता वटिकाभिधाः । त एव वटकाः क्षिप्ताः काञ्जिके काञ्जिकाभिधाः ॥ १४०४ ॥ यत्र यत्र द्रवद्रव्ये तन्नाम्ना वटकास्तु ते ।
english: *Ghārikās* cooked without holes, thrown into *mathita* joined with sugar and combined with cardamom and pepper, are the ones named *vaṭikā*. Those same *vaṭakas*, thrown into *kāñjika*, are the ones named *kāñjika*. In whatever liquid substance they are put, the *vaṭakas* take their name from that. [`मथित` is the chapter's own technical grade, defined at 1571: curd churned and stripped of its butter, with no water added — diluted by half it is *udaśvit*, by a quarter *takra*. At 1404b the manuscripts read `वटिकाभिधाः` and the editor corrects to `वटकाभिधाः`, matching `वटकाः` in the next hemistich; the manuscript reading is kept here.]

latin: आरनालेन सान्द्रेण दध्ना सुमथितेन च ॥ १४०५ ॥ सैन्धवार्द्रकधान्याकजीरकं च विमिश्रयेत् । मरिचानि द्विधा कृत्वा क्षिपेत्तत्र तु पाकवित् ॥ १४०६ ॥ दर्व्या विघट्टयन्सर्वं पचेद्यावद्घनीभवेत् । उत्तार्य वटकान्क्षिप्त्वा विकिरेन्मारिचं रजः ॥ १४०७ ॥ हिङ्गुना धूपयेत्सम्यग्वटकास्ते मनोभिधाः ।
english: With thick *āranāla* and with well-churned curd: one should mix in rock salt, fresh ginger, *dhānyāka* [coriander], and cumin; and the knower of cooking should split the peppercorns in two and throw them in there. Breaking the whole of it up with a ladle, he should cook it until it grows thick. Having taken it off the fire and thrown in the *vaṭakas*, he should scatter pepper powder over them, and smoke them well with asafoetida. Those *vaṭakas* are *mano-abhidhāḥ*. [`आरनालेन` — four syllables, the standard word for thick sour fermented rice gruel, which is the *kāñjika* of 1404; `सान्द्रेण`, thick, is the reading. The peppercorns are cracked in two, and the pepper *powder* at 1407d is a second, separate application. 1408b: the edition prints `मनोभिधाः`, where the transcription behind the recipe pages has `मनोहराः`, "delightful". The `-अभिधाः` formula continues 1404's `वटिकाभिधाः` and `काञ्जिकाभिधाः`, and 1405ab has just said the name follows the liquid, so the sense is plausibly that these *vaṭakas* are named at will; the name-word itself is obscure. MS A reads `मना-`.]

latin: दुग्धमुत्क्वाथ्य तन्मध्ये तक्रमम्लं विनिक्षिपेत् ॥ १४०८ ॥ हित्वा तोयं घनीभूतं वस्त्रबद्धं पृथक्कृतम् । शालितण्डुलपिष्टेन मिश्रितं परिपेषितम् ॥ १४०९ ॥ नानाकारैः सुघटितं सर्पिषा परिपाचितम् । पक्वशर्करया सिक्तमेलाचूर्णेन वासितम् ॥ १४१० ॥ क्षीरप्रकारनामेदं भक्ष्यं मृष्टं मनोहरम् ।
english: Having boiled up milk, one should throw sour *takra* [buttermilk] into the middle of it. The water abandoned, the thickened mass is tied up in cloth and set apart; mixed with the flour of *śāli* rice and thoroughly ground; well formed into various shapes; thoroughly cooked in ghee; drenched with cooked sugar; and scented with cardamom powder. This *bhakṣya*, named *kṣīraprakāra*, is delicious and delightful. [The milk is broken with sour buttermilk, not with a sharp acid. *Śāli* is the fine white rice whose eight varieties open the chapter at 1345–48. "Cooked sugar" is defined immediately below at 1413–14.]

latin: शर्करां वारिसंयुक्तां ताम्रपात्रे विपाचयेत् ॥ १४११ ॥ अर्धपाके क्षिपेद्दुग्धं तक्रं वापि यथारुचि । तेन मुञ्चेन्मलं सा तु शर्करा कथिता सती ॥ १४१२ ॥ निर्मलेन च वस्त्रेण गालयेत्तां मुहुर्मुहुः । मृदौ पाके द्रुता पेया मध्यमे मधुसन्निभा ॥ १४१३ ॥ खरे तु कठिना भक्ष्या साधिके शर्करा भवेत् । खरपाके सुसिद्धायाः सिताया दृढसम्पुटे ॥ १४१४ ॥ नानारूपाणि कुर्वीत खण्डपाकविशारदः । शोधितायां सितायां तु क्षीरं संमिश्रयेत्समम् ॥ १४१५ ॥ खरपाकावधिर्यावत्तावत्तत्क्वाथयेत्पुनः । उत्तार्य नागरं तीक्ष्णमेलाकर्पूरकेसरैः ॥ १४१६ ॥ निक्षिप्य गोलकाः कार्या नाम्ना वर्षोलकास्तु ते ।
english: One should cook *śarkarā* mixed with water in a copper vessel. At the half-cooking one should throw in milk, or else *takra* [buttermilk], as one prefers; by this it releases its impurity, and that *śarkarā*, thus boiled, is the pure one. And one should strain it through a spotless cloth again and again. At the soft cooking it is fluid, a drink; at the middle, it resembles honey; at the hard, it is firm, a *bhakṣya*; and cooked beyond that, it becomes *śarkarā* [it grains back]. Out of *sitā* well perfected at the hard cooking, in a tight *sampuṭa*, the expert in *khaṇḍa*-cooking should make various forms. But into purified *sitā* he should mix an equal measure of milk, and boil that again up to the limit of the hard cooking. Taking it off the fire, [and adding] dry ginger, *tīkṣṇa*, cardamom, camphor, and saffron — having thrown these in, balls are to be made, and by name those are *varṣolakas*. [1412b reads `तक्रं`, buttermilk, which resolves the second clarifying agent: milk or buttermilk thrown into the half-cooked syrup carries the scum up. 1412d prints `सती`, "genuine, pure"; the following verses call the refined product `सिता`. 1414d reads `सिताया दृढसम्पुटे` — MS A has `पञ्चसम्पुटैः`; a *sampuṭa* is a closed two-part vessel, hence a mould, and this is a second product in the passage: hard-stage *sitā* moulded on its own, with no milk and no spice. 1416b reads `तावत्तत्क्वाथयेत्पुनः`, "he should boil that again". `खरपाकावधि`, "up to the limit of the hard cooking", is a stop instruction, and `साधिके शर्करा भवेत्` says what happens past it; the same terminal graining is stated of reduced milk at 1567.]

latin: वराहपललं स्निग्धं मृष्टं सारङ्गजं पलम् ॥ १४१७ ॥ हरिणस्यामिषं पथ्यं रूक्षं मांसं शशोद्भवम् । आविकं तरसं रुच्यं लघु क्रव्यमजोद्भवम् ॥ १४१८ ॥ मत्स्यमांसं भवेद्वृष्यं शाकुनं लघु कीर्तितम् । रुरुसम्वरसंभूतं पुष्टं चेद्रुच्यमीरितम् ॥ १४१९ ॥ मांसान्यन्यानि बल्यानि रसनाप्रीतिदानि च ।
english: The flesh of the pig is unctuous; the flesh born of the *sāraṅga* [the spotted antelope] is fine. The meat of the *hariṇa* deer is wholesome; the flesh arising from the hare is dry. Sheep's flesh is *tarasa* [invigorating] and tasty; the flesh arising from the goat is light. Fish flesh is aphrodisiac; the flesh of birds is declared light. That which comes from the *ruru* and the *sambara* deer, if the animal is well-fed, is said to be tasty. Other meats are strengthening, and give pleasure to the tongue. [1417c: the edition prints `वराहपलळं`, with a doubled *la* (the second written ळ, as this volume regularly writes intervocalic *la*); normalized to ल it is `वराहपललं`, and the doubled syllable is what makes the pāda scan at eight. The sense is simply *varāha-palaṃ*, pig's flesh. Not emended. At 1418d the manuscripts read `क्रव्यमृ-` and the editor corrects to `क्रव्यम-`, giving `क्रव्यम् अजोद्भवम्`, "the flesh arising from the goat"; the corrected reading is printed here.]

latin: कृशस्य व्याधियुक्तस्य जराजर्जरितस्य च ॥ १४२० ॥ शावकस्य च शुष्कस्य विषसन्दूषितस्य च । वारिणा निहतस्यापि श्रमशोषमृतस्य च ॥ १४२१ ॥ क्लिन्नस्य पूतिगन्धस्य मांसानि परिवर्जयेत् ।
english: But of an animal that is emaciated, that is diseased, that is worn out with old age, that is still a suckling, that is dried up, that has been corrupted by poison, that has been killed by water [drowned], that has died of exhaustion and wasting, that is sodden, or that smells putrid — the flesh of these one should avoid altogether.

latin: पृष्ठवंशस्य पार्श्वस्थं बहिरन्तश्च संस्थितम् ॥ १४२२ ॥ जघनस्य घनं पिण्डं पुच्छमूलसमुद्भवम् । क्रोडदेशोद्भवं चैव कक्षाभागस्य पूरकम् ॥ १४२३ ॥ पार्श्वयोः संस्थितं चैव कुक्षिसन्धौ विलेपकम् । अंसपूर्वांशसंभूतं मुकुलं हृदयोद्भवम् ॥ १४२४ ॥ कालखण्डं तथा वृक्को गुदान्त्रं च तथान्त्रकम् । अक्षिणी रसनाकर्णौ वृधो वृषणकर्णकम् ॥ १४२५ ॥ पशुकायां सुसंलग्नं वपामास्तिष्कमज्जकम् । पादाः शृङ्गखुरास्त्वक् च श्रेष्ठमेतत्पलं मतम् ॥ १४२६ ॥
english: That which lies alongside the backbone, both what is placed outside it and what is placed within; the dense lump of the haunch; that which arises at the root of the tail; that which arises in the region of the chest; the filling of the flank portion; that which lies in the two sides; the *vilepaka* at the joint of the belly; that which arises from the shoulder and the fore-quarter; the "bud" (*mukula*) that arises from the heart; the *kālakhaṇḍa* [liver], likewise the kidney, the rectum-and-gut, and the entrails as well; the two eyes, the tongue and the two ears, *vṛdho*, the testicles and the *karṇaka*; and, closely attached to the animal's carcass, the caul-fat, the brain, and the marrow; the feet, the horns, the hooves, and the hide — this flesh is reckoned the finest. [At 1424c the manuscripts read `आस्यं`, "mouth", and the editor corrects to `अंस`, "shoulder"; the correction is printed here. At 1425d `वृधो` is obscure — MS A reads `बृधौ`, a dual, which would suit the paired organs on either side of it. At 1426ab the manuscripts read `वपामाष्ठिस्क-` and `मज्जं-`, with the editor's corrections `मास्तिष्क` [brain] and `माज`; the reading printed here follows his correction of the first and keeps `मज्जक` [marrow] for the second, which is what the metre and the sense require.]
